title: Comparing Design Solutions
keyIdea: When two designs try to solve the same problem, test them both in the same way and write down what happens. Repeat each test a few times, because one try can go wrong. Then use the results to say what each design does well (a strength) and what it does badly (a weakness). Choose the design that fits the job best, and make it better by changing one thing and testing again.
familyTip: Fold two paper aeroplanes: one with wide wings and one with thin, pointy wings. Throw each one 3 times from the same spot and mark where it lands with a sock. Which flew further most of the time? Which flew straighter? Ask your child which plane they would pick for a long-distance contest, and one change they would try next.

visual.caption: Does it help make a test fair? Drag each card to a box, or tap the card then a box.

bins: Does not matter for this test
items: How much water is in the tub
Putting marbles in one at a time
The name you give the boat
What day you do the test

lab.caption: Flagship lab: load two foil boats until they sink, make the test fair, repeat it, race the boats, then choose one for the job and improve it.

kid: A design is a plan for something that solves a problem. Two people can make two different designs for the same job, like two boats to carry marbles.

To find out which works better, test both. Do each test the same way, so only the design is different. That is a fair test. Test more than once. One try can go wrong. If one result is far from the others, test again to check it.
Look at what the tests show. A strength is a thing a design does well. A weakness is a thing it does badly. Most designs have both.
Pick the design that fits the job. Then make it better. Change one thing, test it again and see if it helped.
adult: Ages 5 to 8. This is NGSS K-2-ETS1-3: analyse data from tests of two objects built to solve the same problem, and compare the strengths and weaknesses of each. In England, Key Stage 1 science asks children to do simple tests, gather and record data, and use what they see to suggest answers. Key words: design, problem, test, fair test, data, result, compare, strength, weakness, improve.

Common mistakes: picking the design they like, or the one that looks bigger, not the one the data backs. Trusting a single test. Changing more than one thing between tests, so they cannot tell what made the difference. Thinking one design must win at everything. Adding the two results when the question asks how many more.

Keep the measures concrete and countable at this age: marbles held, seconds to cross, number of throws that landed in a hoop. Help your child put the results in a simple table or bar chart before deciding.

In the lab your child loads two foil boats until each sinks, fixes an unfair test, repeats it three times and spots the odd result, races the boats to find each one's strength and weakness, then chooses a boat for the job and improves it with one change.

practice.prompt: Two boats are tested. Boat A holds 12 marbles. Boat B holds 7. Which boat is stronger?
practice.explain: Boat A held 12 marbles and Boat B held 7, so Boat A can carry more weight.

practice.prompt: Boat A held {a} marbles. Boat B held {b} marbles. How many more did Boat A hold?
practice.hint: How many more means find the gap: take the smaller number away from the bigger one.
practice.explain: {a} take away {b} is {=a-b}. Boat A held {=a-b} more marbles than Boat B.

practice.prompt: Mo tests his paper plane once. It falls straight down. What should he do next?
choices: Throw it a few more times the same way
Say it is a bad plane
practice.hint: Can one try go wrong? What would show what the plane usually does?
practice.explain: One test can go wrong. Testing a few more times shows what the plane usually does.

practice.prompt: A tower of cups stood for {a} seconds. A tower of blocks stood {b} seconds longer. How long did the block tower stand?
practice.hint: The block tower lasted longer, so add the extra seconds.
practice.explain: {a} add {b} is {=a+b} seconds. The block tower stood for {=a+b} seconds.

practice.prompt: To test which umbrella keeps a teddy drier, what should be the same for both umbrellas?
choices: The amount of water poured on them
practice.hint: What could make one teddy wetter even if the umbrellas were the same?
practice.explain: Pour the same amount of water on each. Then only the umbrella design is different, so the test is fair.

pool.prompt: What is a weakness of a design?
pool.hint: A strength is something it does well. A weakness is the opposite.
pool.explain: A weakness is something a design does badly, like a boat that is slow.

pool.prompt: Boat A holds 12 marbles but is slow. Boat B is fast but holds 7. You must carry 10 marbles. Which boat?
pool.hint: Boat B holds 7. Can it carry 10 without sinking?
pool.explain: Only Boat A can hold 10 marbles. Boat B would sink, even though it is faster.

pool.prompt: A plane flew 5 steps, then 6 steps, then 1 step. Which result does not fit?
pool.hint: Look for the result far from the others.
pool.explain: 1 step is far from 5 and 6. Something went wrong in that throw, so test again to check it.

pool.prompt: Ana wants her boat to go faster. She adds a sail and makes it bigger and paints it, all at once. What is the problem?
choices: She cannot tell which change helped
Nothing, that is the best way
pool.hint: How many things did she change?
pool.explain: Change one thing at a time, then test. If you change three things at once, you cannot tell which one helped.

pool.prompt: Tower A stood {a} blocks tall before it fell. Tower B stood {b} blocks tall. How many more blocks did Tower A have?
pool.hint: Find the gap between the two towers.
pool.explain: {a} take away {b} is {=a-b}. Tower A was {=a-b} blocks taller.

pool.prompt: Why do we test both designs in the same way?
choices: So only the design is different
pool.hint: Think about what else could change the result.
pool.explain: If everything else is the same, any difference in the results comes from the design. That is a fair test.

pool.prompt: Boat A held {a}, {a} and {b} marbles in 3 tests. How many marbles did it hold in all?
pool.explain: {a} add {a} add {b} is {=a+a+b} marbles in all.

pool.prompt: Which is a strength of a raincoat design?
choices: It is too heavy to wear
pool.hint: A strength helps the coat do its job.
pool.explain: Keeping you dry is what a raincoat is for, so that is a strength. Ripping and being heavy are weaknesses.

pool.prompt: Sam likes the tall cup boat best, but the wide tray held more marbles. How should he choose a boat for a heavy load?
pool.hint: Look at the test results, not at which boat you like best.
pool.explain: Use the test results. The wide tray held more, so it is the better choice for a heavy load.
